metric.semantic_locality.aggregation_note: Sum of required lookups across the 44 probes = 23; mean = 23/44 = 0.5227 lookups/probe; normalized Semantic Locality score for Swift = 100*44/(44+23) = 4400/67 = 65.67 (higher is better, i.e. fewer required non-local lookups).
metric.semantic_locality.basis: all-fragments (Swift-only shard, 44/44 probes assigned a fragment or documented substitute). Cross-language common-basis reconciliation (probes for which ALL TEN languages have a fragment) is runner-only per interaction_with_quality_metrics.common_basis_rule; this shard supplies Swift's raw per-probe lookup counts for that reconciliation.
metric.semantic_locality.methodology_citation: semantic_compression.md section 6.1.3.C 'Semantic Locality': raw measurement is the number of required external semantic lookups/declaration-graph hops needed to resolve the frozen semantic facts of each probe from the local surface form alone. Lower is better. Only lookups required (not optional/extra-detail lookups) are counted; the lookup vocabulary used (callee signature, variable declaration, type declaration, overload set, trait/interface/protocol implementation, imported definition, global configuration/compiler mode) is illustrative ('such as'), not exhaustive.
metric.semantic_locality.normalization_rule: score = 100 * total_probes / (total_probes + total_required_lookups) = 100 / (1 + mean_lookups_per_probe). Monotonic decreasing in lookup cost, 0 lookups -> 100, 1 lookup/probe on average -> 50. This formula is mechanical, frozen for this measurement, and must be applied identically to every language's raw lookup counts for comparability; it is documented here for that purpose.

per_probe.note: `let n = 7; return n` — literal-inferred Int, let/mutability/init state all explicit local syntax; integer literal type inference is a fixed language rule, not a per-site lookup.
`var counter: Int64 = 0; let LIMIT: Int64 = 100` — var/let and explicit Int64 annotation fully local.
`var v: Int32` uninitialized, two-way if/else assigning both arms, then read; Swift definite-initialization checking is a fixed compiler rule visible from the branch shape itself.
`UnsafeMutablePointer<UInt8>.allocate(capacity:16)` gives uninitialized (not zero-filled) storage; that guarantee is documented on UnsafeMutablePointer, not visible from the call syntax alone.
`x += 1` in-place update; compound assignment semantics are fixed language syntax.
`xs[1] = 42` in-place element mutation through the existing binding; local.

`withUnsafeMutablePointer(to:&slot){port in port.pointee=9}` — that `port` aliases `slot`'s storage for the closure's duration is the documented contract of withUnsafeMutablePointer, not visible from local syntax.
`let window = xs[...]` yields an ArraySlice; that ArraySlice shares storage with `xs` via copy-on-write rather than copying is documented on ArraySlice/Array, not shown by the subscript syntax.
`first === second` — `===` is Swift's fixed reference-identity operator for class instances; its meaning is a core language-defined token, not a per-declaration lookup.
Frozen by the probe's own text: 'f's own declaration is explicitly excluded ... and is counted as a non-local lookup for metric C.' Applies identically to every language including Swift.
Measured fragment for this probe explicitly includes `put`'s full inout declaration and body plus the `&cell` call site, so the writable-alias fact is fully local by construction.

`let neg: (Int32)->Int32 = { a in k - a }` then `xs.map(neg)` — whether `k` is captured by reference to its storage vs by value is governed by Swift's closure-capture semantics, documented in the language reference rather than visible from the capture-less closure syntax.
`func mid(_ xs:[Int32])->Int32{xs[1]}`; Int32 is a value type, so no post-return aliasing is possible — this is intrinsic, fixed language knowledge, not a per-site lookup.
Named tuple return `(q:Int32,r:Int32)` with tuple-destructuring bind; fully explicit local syntax.

`a*b+c`; fixed-width Int32 arithmetic with trapping overflow under the frozen optimized-checked Swift build mode is intrinsic operator semantics, treated like other universally fixed operator behavior.
`a/b`, `a%b`, `Double(a)/Double(b)`; truncating division and dividend-sign remainder are fixed Swift language rules, local.
`m &+ 1` — the wrapping-add operator's behavior is fixed language syntax, fully explicit at the site regardless of build mode.
Explicit local `if b == 0 { q = 0 } else { q = a / b }` guard; fully local.

`s1 == s2` on String is content comparison, but the precise contract (Unicode canonical-equivalence comparison rather than raw byte/UTF-16 comparison) is documented on String's Equatable conformance, not visible from `==` alone.
`xs.sort(by: >)` mutates `xs` in place; that `sort` (vs `sorted`) is the mutating member is a documented API-naming convention, not visible from the call site alone.

`Int32(exactly: big) ?? 0` — that the failable initializer returns nil (rather than trapping) on out-of-range input is the documented contract of `init?(exactly:)`, not derivable from the call syntax alone.
`Double(i) + d` — Swift forbids implicit Int/Double mixing, so the explicit `Double(i)` conversion is fully visible locally.
`xs[i]` traps on out-of-range index; Array provides no optional/checked subscript in the standard library, so trap-on-failure is a fact of Array's subscript declaration, not visible from `[i]` alone.
`xs[1..<4]` yields an ArraySlice sharing storage (COW) with `xs`; same documented-not-syntactic fact as F04.P2.
`let o: Int32? = nil; let n = o ?? 0` — Optional and `??` are core fixed language syntax, fully local.
`o.map(h)` short-circuits to nil on absence and applies `h` on presence; the exact monadic contract of Optional.map is documented on Optional, not fully derivable from the method name alone.
`Int32(s)` is a failable initializer returning `Int32?`; that String-to-Int32 conversion is failable (rather than trapping/throwing) is a fact of Int32's declared initializer overload set.
Same as F13.P1: `Int32(s) ?? 0` relies on the documented failable-initializer contract of Int32(String).
`enum Shape { case circle(r:Double); case rect(w:Double,h:Double) }`; Swift enums are closed by fixed language rule (extensions may add members, never cases) — intrinsic, local.
`switch s { case .circle(let r): ...; case .rect(let w,let h): ... }` with no default arm; compiler-enforced exhaustiveness over enum cases is a fixed, locally visible language rule.

Extensibility requires protocol-based dispatch (`protocol Shape { func area()->Double }`, `Tri: Shape` in a separate unit); that `s.area()` dispatches to `Tri`'s witness at runtime depends on Swift's protocol/witness-table dispatch mechanism, documented rather than visible from the call syntax.
`func head<T>(_ xs:[T])->T { xs[0] }`; the T-to-T relationship is explicit at the generic declaration, fully local.
`func max_of<T: Comparable>(_ a:T,_ b:T)->T` — declaration-site constraint explicit and diagnosed at the generic's own declaration, local.
`let items:[Named] = [A(), B()]; items[0].tag()` — runtime dispatch through the `Named` existential relies on the same documented protocol-witness dispatch mechanism as F14.P3.
`xs.reduce(0, +)` — the fold order/associativity guarantee (left-to-right) is documented on Array/Sequence.reduce, not visible from the call site alone.

`for (_,v) in mp {...}` and `mp["b"] ?? 0` — Dictionary's unspecified iteration order and its Optional-returning subscript are documented facts of Dictionary's declaration, not visible from the loop/subscript syntax alone.

`defer { handle.closeFile() }` immediately after acquisition inside a throwing function; `defer`'s exactly-once, every-exit-path guarantee is fixed core language keyword semantics, local like other control-flow keywords.

`deinit { released += 1 }` on a class value whose only strong reference goes out of scope; the precise deterministic-timing guarantee of ARC-driven deinit (as opposed to a nondeterministic collector) rests on Swift's documented memory-management model, consulted beyond the local declaration.
`print("x")` requires no import, but its signature/behavior (no throw, discards return) is drawn from the implicitly available Swift standard library, not from any local declaration in the fragment.

`private func secret()->Int32` plus `func pub_add(...)` in util.swift (multi-unit recipe), called unqualified as `pub_add(2,3)` from the other file since Swift's module-scoped visibility needs no call-site qualification; `private` file-scoping is a fixed, locally visible language rule.

`async let x = 20; async let y = 22; let sum = await x + y` — that `async let` starts an implicit concurrent child task is documented in Swift's structured-concurrency model, not visible purely from the `async`/`await` tokens.

`actor Counter { var value: Int64 = 0; func increment(){value+=1} }` accessed from two concurrent tasks; the documented, normative race-freedom guarantee for actor-isolated mutable state must be looked up and cited per the probe's own verification requirement.

`import Glibc`/`import Darwin` then `abs(-3)` reaching the platform C library's `abs`; the imported C function's signature, ABI and calling convention come from the bridged platform module, not from local declarations.

`@_cdecl("add2") func add2(_ a:Int32,_ b:Int32)->Int32` — the underscored `@_cdecl` attribute's C-ABI/unmangled-symbol effect is documented only in compiler-level references (it is not part of the public Swift language reference), requiring an external lookup beyond the local declaration.

metric.semantic_locality.worker_conditions: packet-only worker, no compiler/toolchain access available. Measurement was produced by expert manual analysis of documented Swift language/standard-library semantics for each of the 44 frozen probes' canonical_task, using the language-neutral measured_fragment boundaries and the frozen site inventory from semantic_site_matrix.json. This is a documented substitute for mechanical build/run evidence, which is unavailable in this transport; no value was fabricated where analysis was possible for all 44 probes.
